linked.job: Wipes drives completely, with proof it was done.
linked.name: Beerus — Live Boot
linked.note: Beerus's other form: a bootable USB stick of its own — a drive is wiped by booting from the stick, for machines that are off or being decommissioned whole. The Beerus app in this bundle runs the same engine on a machine that is already running. Get the image from the Beerus repo.

notes: Flat layout: every tool's files sit together in this one folder — the bundle adds no per-tool folders of its own. A tool keeps only the structure its own portable edition ships with (Charon's Charon folder, Aegis's Aegis folder, and NitroCore's _internal folder are part of those tools). The one exception the bundle itself makes is Beerus's folder, which exists to answer the _internal collision described below.

One file-name collision, resolved openly: six of the seven portable editions carry a file named README-PORTABLE.txt at their top level, each with different contents. In this bundle each of those is kept as README-PORTABLE-<Tool>.txt — contents unchanged; only the name is qualified, so nothing overwrites anything. The seventh, Aegis's, sits inside its Aegis folder exactly as its portable ships, so it never reaches this folder's level and keeps its own name.

A second collision, resolved openly: Beerus Portable and NitroCore are both one-folder apps whose support folder is named _internal, and both zips put that folder at the top level — two different support folders cannot share one name in one folder. So Beerus sits in a Beerus folder inside this bundle (the same shape Charon ships in): Beerus.exe and its _internal, byte for byte as released; only where they sit is different. Its start file is Beerus/Beerus.exe.

Argus portable mode: starting Argus from the launcher (or from Argus-Portable.bat) keeps its settings, scan history, and quarantine vault in the ArgusData folder inside this folder, so they travel with the bundle.

Beerus Portable keeps its work records beside its own start file: certificates of destruction land in Beerus/certificates, and its file, folder, and free-space wipe reports in Beerus/certificates/reports. They are the technician's job records; they travel with this folder.

Aegis keeps nothing anywhere else: no settings folder, no registry entries, no temporary copies. Its vaults are single sealed files (.aegis) that you name and place yourself — beside the app or anywhere you choose — and nothing about what you copy is ever written to disk; the clipboard clears itself.

Lazarus keeps its backup stores in a folder you name when you create one, and refuses system folders for them. Bringing files back always writes to a different drive than the one being rescued — never to the source. It sends nothing anywhere: no account, no cloud, no telemetry.
Sphinx — the kit's eighth member — is not in this bundle yet: it has no published release to assemble from. It joins at the next assembly after its first release ships.
